t: Find the K-Beauty of a Number
o: Slide a window of length k over the decimal representation of num and count windows whose numeric value is a nonzero divisor of num. Leading zeros are allowed (so "04" evaluates to 4), and 0 never divides. With num ≤ 1e9 the string has at most 10 characters, so any linear scan is instant. Example 1: windows "24","40" both divide 240 → 2. Example 2: "43" divides, "30","00","04" don't, final "43" divides → 2.
k: There are only len(num)-k+1 windows; evaluate each directly.
Skip zero windows explicitly since division by zero is invalid.
Rolling arithmetic (drop leading digit, append next) avoids repeated substring-to-int conversion.

a.i: Convert num to a string and test every length-k substring: parse it, and if it is nonzero and num mod value == 0, count it.
s: For each i from 0 to len(s)-k, take v = int(s[i:i+k]).
Count v if v != 0 and num % v == 0.
a.t: O(d·k) where d ≤ 10 digits — constant in practice.

a.i: Avoid strings entirely: take the last k digits as the first window, then roll by cur = (cur mod 10^(k-1)) * 10 + next digit, walking digits from least significant to most significant.
s: Extract digits of num into an array (or process via powers of 10).
Initialize cur to the lowest k digits.
At each step test divisibility, then roll: cur = cur % 10^(k-1) * 10 + nextDigit.
Continue until the highest digit is consumed.
a.t: O(d) — each digit processed once with O(1) work.
a.sp: O(d) for the digit buffer (O(1) if processed via modulo directly).

w: Both approaches are trivially fast given the tiny input; the string version is preferable for clarity. Pitfalls: dividing by zero ("00" windows) and off-by-one on the window count. Follow-up: what if num had thousands of digits? Then the rolling approach with big-integer mod is required.
